help.data.title: About the data
help.data:
Source: U.S. Department of Education, College Scorecard, released June 2026.
Programs: degrees awarded in 2021-22 and 2022-23. Program earnings: graduates of 2018-20 with federal aid, measured 1 year later.
Cost before aid and average paid after grants: 2023-24. Tuition and fees: 2024-25.
Admission rates, test policies, enrollment and students per faculty: fall 2024.
Completion and transfer rates: students who started in 2018 (four-year colleges) or 2021 (two-year colleges).
Interests and careers: U.S. Department of Labor, O*NET 31.0 (CC BY 4.0). Links between careers and programs: NCES and BLS CIP-SOC crosswalk (CIP 2020, SOC 2018); a link means a program prepares for a career, not that graduates work in it.
Public and private colleges are included; for-profit colleges are not. Program records and outcomes describe colleges; they do not measure academic quality.

pri.title: What matters most to you?
pri.subtitle: Choose what matters most. We'll use your priorities to organize your options.
pri.desc.COSTS: I want to understand what students pay after grants and scholarships.
pri.desc.GRADUATION: I care about how many students finish their degree.
pri.desc.ADMISSION: I want colleges with open or less selective admission.
pri.desc.STUDY: I want to explore colleges that offer programs related to my interests.
pri.desc.CAMPUS: Location, setting and size matter to me.
pri.basis.COSTS: Uses the average amount students with federal aid paid after grants (historical; your income range if you gave it). It is a reference, not your personal price. Public colleges outside your home state are not compared on this, because their averages use in-state rates.
pri.basis.GRADUATION: Uses the completion rate: four-year colleges within 6 years, two-year colleges within 3 years. The two are measured differently and are only compared with the same kind of college. It does not predict your own outcome.
pri.basis.ADMISSION: Uses open admission and the admission rate for all applicants. It describes the college, not your chances.
pri.basis.STUDY: We use historical degree records to find colleges with programs related to your interests: more of your chosen programs first, then degree levels that fit your plans. This does not measure program quality.
pri.basis.CAMPUS: Uses your campus choices from the previous step: states, setting and size.

order.how.title: How colleges are ordered
order.how.evidence: Colleges with records of your programs come first (when you chose programs).
order.how.COSTS: College costs: lower average cost after grants first. Costs within $1,000 count as a tie. Costs that cannot be compared (out-of-state public colleges, or not reported) go last.
order.how.GRADUATION: Graduation outcomes: higher completion rate first. Rates within 5 points count as a tie. Rates measured differently or not reported go last.
order.how.ADMISSION: Admission accessibility: open admission first, then higher admission rates. Rates within 10 points count as a tie.
order.how.STUDY: Programs related to your interests: colleges offering more of your chosen programs first, then degree levels that fit your plans.
order.how.CAMPUS: Campus environment: colleges matching more of your campus choices first.
order.how.degrees: If still tied: more degrees awarded in your programs (program size, not quality).
order.how.name: If still tied: college name.
order.how.note: Each group (community, four-year public, private) is ordered separately. There is no overall score.

web.grade.9.1: Ask your counselor how classes from your previous school count toward graduation.
web.grade.9.2: Take the hardest classes you can, and use English language support if your school offers it.
web.grade.9.3: Try a club, sport, job or volunteer work. Colleges look at activities too.
web.grade.10.1: Check with your counselor that you are on track with credits and required exams.
web.grade.10.2: Take the PSAT if your school offers it. It is practice, and colleges do not see it.
web.grade.10.3: Look for summer programs, jobs or volunteer work.
web.grade.11.1: Find out whether the colleges on your list want SAT or ACT scores; many do not require them.
web.grade.11.2: Visit colleges in person or online, and write down what you like.
web.grade.11.3: Think of two teachers who know you well and could write recommendation letters.
web.grade.11.4: Ask a counselor which financial aid you can apply for.
web.grade.12.1: Make a list of application deadlines; many are between November and February.
web.grade.12.2: Ask for recommendation letters at least a month before a deadline.
web.grade.12.3: Ask about application fee waivers if cost is a concern.
web.grade.12.4: Ask staff which financial aid forms apply to you, and complete them early.
web.grade.12.5: Many community colleges accept applications later in the year. Check their deadlines and placement tests.
